---
title: Introduction
description: Share cached release metadata with your desktop and mobile update clients.
---

Upserve is a self-hostable application update server. It sits between your release repository and your installed applications, so every update check doesn't need its own request to GitHub.

You publish releases and signed artifacts as usual. Upserve finds the right release, caches its metadata and answers your application's update protocol. Public downloads redirect to GitHub by default. Private downloads pass through your server after you authorize the request.

## When to use Upserve

Use Upserve when you want a stable update endpoint, shared caching or one place to manage release channels across several applications. You can run it as a standalone service or add its Hono application to a server you already have.

It works with:

- **Tauri v2**, using your existing updater manifests and signatures.
- **electron-builder and electron-updater**, using the generic provider feed.
- **Android APKs**, using an Upserve JSON manifest and your own update client.
- **Custom applications**, using the generic JSON API or an adapter you write.

Upserve doesn't build your app, sign it or generate binary patches. Your release pipeline and updater remain responsible for those tasks. It caches update metadata, not installer binaries.

## Start here

Follow the [quick start](/docs/quick-start) to run a server and make your first update request. You'll need Node.js 22.13 or newer and a GitHub repository with a published release. Node.js 24 is recommended for the standalone service and SQLite cache.

Already have an updater? Start with [Tauri](/docs/tauri), [Electron](/docs/electron), [Android](/docs/android) or [custom applications](/docs/generic). Each guide includes the server setup and the client endpoint.

## A note about availability

The installation commands in these guides use the intended public package names. During initial private development, the packages might not be on npm yet. If installation returns a package-not-found error, use the [repository checkout instructions](/docs/quick-start#run-from-a-repository-checkout).


---
title: Quick start
description: Install Upserve, start a Node.js server and check a GitHub release.
---

import { Tab, Tabs } from "fumadocs-ui/components/tabs";

import { Step, Steps } from "fumadocs-ui/components/steps";

This guide runs an update server for an application called **Editor**. Its application ID is `editor`, and its release repository is `owner/editor`. Replace `owner/editor` with your own public GitHub repository everywhere it appears.

You'll need Node.js 22.13 or newer, a package manager and at least one published release with a semantic version tag such as `v1.2.0`. You don't need a database or a GitHub token for a public repository.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Install the server packages

In a new project directory, create a `package.json` if you don't have one:

```sh
npm init -y
```

Then install the packages with your preferred package manager.

<Tabs items={["npm", "pnpm", "Yarn", "Bun"]}>

<Tab value="npm">

```sh
npm install @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="pnpm">

```sh
pnpm add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Yarn">

```sh
yarn add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Bun">

```sh
bun add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

</Tabs>

The core handles release selection and caching. The GitHub package reads releases, the generic adapter exposes JSON endpoints, and the Hono Node adapter starts the HTTP listener.

</Step>
<Step>

### Create your server

Save this as `server.ts`. The generic API lets you verify the server before connecting a framework-specific updater.

```ts title="server.ts"
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";
import { createUpserve } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

const updates = createUpserve({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [generic()],
    },
  },
});

serve({ fetch: updates.fetch, port: 3000 });
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Start it

```sh
npx tsx server.ts
```

This command uses `tsx` to run TypeScript. The library example doesn't print a startup banner. Leave it running and open another terminal.

</Step>
<Step>

### Make an update request

First, check the configured channels. This request doesn't contact GitHub:

```sh
curl http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/generic/channels
```

```json
{ "channels": ["stable", "prerelease"] }
```

Now request your latest stable release:

```sh
curl -i http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/generic/latest
```

For a published `v1.2.0` release, the JSON includes `"version": "1.2.0"` and the release assets. If there are no matching published releases, you'll receive `204 No Content`. A `503` usually means GitHub couldn't be reached or the repository isn't accessible. See [error responses](/docs/errors).

</Step>
<Step>

### Connect your updater

Use the [Tauri](/docs/tauri), [Electron](/docs/electron) or [Android](/docs/android) guide to add that adapter and configure your client. For your own client, request `/editor/stable/generic/update/1.0.0` and follow the [generic API guide](/docs/generic).

Use HTTPS when you deploy. See [standalone and Docker deployment](/docs/deployment) if you'd rather run a service than maintain this small server file.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Run from a repository checkout

Before the packages are published, clone the Upserve repository using an account with access. From its root, run:

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build
pnpm exec tsx apps/playground/index.ts
```

The playground uses local fixtures, so you can check `/demo/stable/generic/latest` without GitHub credentials. For your own repository, edit `examples/upserve.config.ts` and start the workspace CLI:

```sh
UPSERVE_CONFIG=examples/upserve.config.ts pnpm exec tsx packages/cli/src/index.ts start
```

See [CLI configuration](/docs/deployment#configuration-file) for environment variables and startup output.


---
title: How Upserve works
description: Follow an update check from your application to a cached release and download.
---

An update check has two parts: deciding which release to offer and downloading its installer. Upserve caches the information needed for the first part. It redirects or streams the download for the second.

## Follow an update check

1. Your app requests an endpoint such as `/editor/stable/tauri/darwin/aarch64/1.0.0`.
2. Upserve checks your access rule, if you've configured one.
3. It looks for cached release metadata. If it needs fresh data, it asks the release provider.
4. The adapter checks the selected release's manifest and answers in your updater's format.
5. Your updater downloads the asset using the returned URL and verifies it before installation.

If several clients check at once, Upserve fetches the same metadata once and shares the result between them. See [caching](/docs/cache) for expiry, outages and rate limits.

## The pieces you configure

| Piece       | What it does                                                 | Built-in choices                       |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| Application | Groups one app's releases, access rules and update protocols | Your entries in `apps`                 |
| Provider    | Reads releases and opens known assets                        | GitHub Releases                        |
| Adapter     | Implements the HTTP protocol your updater expects            | Tauri, Electron, Android, generic JSON |
| Cache store | Saves release and manifest metadata                          | Memory, optional SQLite                |

An application can expose several adapters. For example, your desktop and Android builds can share a repository and application ID while using different manifests.

## Versions, tags and IDs

For a GitHub release tagged `v1.2.0`, the **version** is `1.2.0`, the **tag** is `v1.2.0`, and the **ID** is GitHub's release identifier. They serve different purposes. Upserve compares semantic versions to select updates; it doesn't compare GitHub IDs or publication dates.

The default `stable` channel excludes releases marked as prereleases. The default `prerelease` channel includes only those releases. [Channels](/docs/channels) explains how to change that selection.

## What stays in your release pipeline

Keep building installers, generating checksums and signing updates in your existing pipeline. Upload the original manifest and every artifact it references to the same release. Upserve doesn't need signing private keys and doesn't generate signatures.

Adapters validate the selected release before offering it. If its manifest is incomplete, Upserve returns an error rather than silently trying an older release. Correct the release assets, then refresh or wait for cache expiry.


---
title: Choose an integration
description: Find the guide for your existing updater without changing its release protocol.
---

Choose the guide that matches the updater already installed in your application. Each guide walks through the packages, release assets, server setup and client configuration.

| Your application                            | Guide                                | What you publish                                 |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Tauri v2 desktop app                        | [Tauri](/docs/tauri)                 | `latest.json`, signed updater artifacts          |
| electron-builder app using electron-updater | [Electron](/docs/electron)           | Platform YAML, installers and existing blockmaps |
| Android app distributed outside Google Play | [Android](/docs/android)             | `latest-android.json` and an APK                 |
| CLI, desktop app or another custom client   | [Custom applications](/docs/generic) | Release assets; no adapter manifest required     |

Electron's native `autoUpdater` uses other protocols and isn't supported by the Electron adapter. Android doesn't have a universal sideloaded update protocol, so you'll implement the client check and installation flow yourself.

Need a different protocol? You can [write an adapter](/docs/custom-adapters) without changing Upserve. You don't need to understand the extension contracts to use a built-in integration.


---
title: Tauri
description: Connect a Tauri v2 updater to Upserve while keeping your existing signatures.
---

import { Tab, Tabs } from "fumadocs-ui/components/tabs";

import { Step, Steps } from "fumadocs-ui/components/steps";

Upserve serves the Tauri v2 updater protocol. Keep your current updater plugin and signing setup; change its endpoint to your Upserve server.

This guide assumes you already build signed Tauri updates. If not, follow the [Tauri updater setup](https://v2.tauri.app/plugin/updater/) first. Upserve never needs your signing private key.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Prepare your release

Publish a GitHub release such as `v1.2.0` in `owner/editor`. Upload:

- `latest.json`, using Tauri's static manifest format.
- Every updater binary referenced in its `platforms` object.
- The signatures produced by your existing build, included in that manifest.

For example, the `darwin-aarch64` entry should point to the Apple Silicon updater artifact from this same release. A manifest URL must exactly match the asset's GitHub download URL. Ordinary installers aren't always updater artifacts; use the files Tauri generates for the updater.

A static manifest has this shape. Replace the repository, artifact name and signature with the values produced by your release pipeline; `SIGNATURE_FROM_CI` isn't a usable signature.

```json title="latest.json"
{
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "platforms": {
    "darwin-aarch64": {
      "url": "https://github.com/owner/editor/releases/download/v1.2.0/editor.app.tar.gz",
      "signature": "SIGNATURE_FROM_CI"
    }
  }
}
```

Upserve checks the manifest version against the release version, requires nonempty signatures and checks that all referenced binaries exist. It preserves signature strings and replaces download URLs with server asset URLs. Notes and publication date come from the release metadata.

</Step>
<Step>

### Install and configure Upserve

<Tabs items={["npm", "pnpm", "Yarn", "Bun"]}>

<Tab value="npm">

```sh
npm install @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-tauri @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="pnpm">

```sh
pnpm add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-tauri @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Yarn">

```sh
yarn add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-tauri @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Bun">

```sh
bun add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-tauri @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

</Tabs>

Replace `owner/editor` with your repository.

```ts title="server.ts"
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";
import { createUpserve } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { tauri } from "@neplex/upserve-tauri";

const updates = createUpserve({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [tauri()],
    },
  },
});

serve({ fetch: updates.fetch, port: 3000 });
```

If your manifest has another filename, use `tauri({ manifest: "updater.json" })`.

</Step>
<Step>

### Set the updater endpoint

In your existing `src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`, set the endpoint while keeping your real public key:

```json title="src-tauri/tauri.conf.json (updater section)"
{
  "plugins": {
    "updater": {
      "pubkey": "YOUR_EXISTING_TAURI_PUBLIC_KEY",
      "endpoints": [
        "https://updates.example.com/editor/stable/tauri/{{target}}/{{arch}}/{{current_version}}"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Replace `updates.example.com` with your deployed host. Keep your existing plugin registration and permissions. No new update-check implementation is required. Use HTTPS; Tauri's development HTTP opt-in is only for local testing.

</Step>
<Step>

### Start and test

```sh
npx tsx server.ts
curl -i http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/tauri/darwin/aarch64/1.0.0
```

With a valid `1.2.0` release for that platform, you'll receive `200` with `version`, `signature`, `url` and any available `notes` and `pub_date`. The signature is the one you published. A current version of `1.2.0`, or a missing `darwin-aarch64` platform, returns `204 No Content`.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Static manifest clients

`/editor/stable/tauri/latest.json` returns a static manifest with a `platforms` object. Use this endpoint for clients that need static manifest selection, including custom target keys. The dynamic endpoint constructs the key as `target-arch` and doesn't interpret custom target naming conventions.

## If your update isn't detected

Compare the target and architecture in your request with the exact key in `latest.json`, such as `windows-x86_64` or `linux-x86_64`. Confirm the requested version is older and the release belongs to the chosen [channel](/docs/channels).

A missing manifest returns `404`. Invalid JSON, an empty signature, a version mismatch or a referenced binary outside the selected release returns `422` when there's no usable cached manifest. See [troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) for cache and refresh checks.


---
title: Electron
description: Serve electron-updater generic feeds, original YAML and differential download assets.
---

import { Tab, Tabs } from "fumadocs-ui/components/tabs";

import { Step, Steps } from "fumadocs-ui/components/steps";

This adapter supports **electron-builder applications using electron-updater's generic provider**. Electron's native `autoUpdater` uses protocols such as Squirrel and isn't interchangeable with electron-updater. Squirrel and Sparkle aren't supported by this adapter.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Keep your electron-builder artifacts

For each published release in `owner/editor`, upload electron-builder's original YAML and the files it references. Depending on your targets, those include:

| Platform | Feed filename                                 | Typical artifacts                       |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Windows  | `latest.yml`                                  | NSIS installer and `.blockmap`          |
| macOS    | `latest-mac.yml`                              | ZIP, DMG and generated blockmaps        |
| Linux    | `latest-linux.yml` or `latest-linux-ARCH.yml` | Target artifacts and generated metadata |

Use a tag such as `v1.2.0`. The YAML `version` must equal `1.2.0`. Each entry in `files` needs a SHA-512 base64 checksum and a positive file size matching the GitHub asset. File URLs must be relative basenames in the same release.

Upserve returns the YAML unchanged. It doesn't regenerate checksums, re-sign metadata or create differential patches. Preserve your existing platform signing and electron-updater verification.

</Step>
<Step>

### Install and configure the server

<Tabs items={["npm", "pnpm", "Yarn", "Bun"]}>

<Tab value="npm">

```sh
npm install @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-electron @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="pnpm">

```sh
pnpm add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-electron @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Yarn">

```sh
yarn add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-electron @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Bun">

```sh
bun add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-electron @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

</Tabs>

```ts title="server.ts"
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";
import { createUpserve } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { electron } from "@neplex/upserve-electron";

const updates = createUpserve({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [electron()],
    },
  },
});

serve({ fetch: updates.fetch, port: 3000 });
```

Replace `owner/editor` with your repository.

</Step>
<Step>

### Configure electron-updater

Install `electron-updater` in your Electron application if it isn't already installed. In electron-builder's configuration, set a generic feed:

```yaml title="electron-builder.yml (publish section)"
publish:
  provider: generic
  url: https://updates.example.com/editor/stable/electron/
  useMultipleRangeRequest: false
```

Replace the example host. Keep the trailing slash. Continue calling `autoUpdater.checkForUpdatesAndNotify()` from **electron-updater** in your main process. This is a focused client snippet for an already configured Electron application:

```ts
import { autoUpdater } from "electron-updater";

autoUpdater.checkForUpdatesAndNotify();
```

If you configure the feed at runtime instead, pass the same `provider`, `url` and `useMultipleRangeRequest` to `autoUpdater.setFeedURL()`.

</Step>
<Step>

### Start and test the feed

```sh
npx tsx server.ts
curl -i http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/electron/latest.yml
```

Use `latest-mac.yml` or your Linux filename to test those targets. Expect `200` and the original YAML. Test the packaged app too; successful YAML retrieval alone doesn't prove signing, installation or differential download behavior on each operating system.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Differential downloads

Electron-updater can download only the parts of an installer that changed when you publish its existing blockmap data. Upserve makes the installer and blockmaps available and forwards the client's download requests. It doesn't generate those files.

GitHub delivery supports single byte ranges. Set `useMultipleRangeRequest: false` so the client doesn't request multipart ranges. Keep the old release's blockmaps in the repository because a client upgrading from that release may request them. A reverse proxy must forward `Range` and preserve `206 Partial Content` responses. See [asset delivery](/docs/assets).

## Prerelease feeds

For a `beta` YAML prefix on the default `prerelease` channel, configure `electron({ channels: { prerelease: "beta" } })` and point your prerelease clients at `/editor/prerelease/electron/`. The `channels` option maps URL channel names to YAML filename prefixes; it doesn't select releases. [Release channels](/docs/channels) controls selection.

## Supported configurations and limits

NSIS installers, macOS ZIP/DMG feeds and Linux feeds with relative asset filenames are the intended configurations. Architecture-specific Linux YAML suffixes are accepted; every artifact referenced by a feed still needs to be in that release.

Web installers using a YAML `packages` field, absolute external file URLs and alternate signed feed envelopes aren't supported. A missing feed returns `404`; malformed YAML, missing artifacts or mismatched checksums/sizes return `422` without a usable cached manifest. Upserve validates checksum format, not the binary's digest. Electron-updater must verify the actual download.

For client details, see the [electron-builder auto-update guide](https://www.electron.build/docs/features/auto-update/) and [generic provider implementation](https://github.com/electron-userland/electron-builder/blob/master/packages/electron-updater/src/providers/GenericProvider.ts).


---
title: Android
description: Publish APK update metadata and connect your own Android update client.
---

import { Tab, Tabs } from "fumadocs-ui/components/tabs";

import { Step, Steps } from "fumadocs-ui/components/steps";

Android has no universal updater protocol for apps distributed outside Google Play. Upserve supplies a JSON manifest and an APK download URL. Your app decides when to check, verifies the download and uses Android's supported installation flow with the user's consent.

You don't give Upserve your APK signing keys. Keep signing APKs in your existing release pipeline.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Publish the APK and its manifest

Upload your signed `editor.apk` and `latest-android.json` to the same GitHub release, such as `v1.2.0` in `owner/editor`.

```json title="latest-android.json"
{
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "versionCode": 12,
  "notes": "Fixes startup on Android 15.",
  "pub_date": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "android": {
    "url": "https://github.com/owner/editor/releases/download/v1.2.0/editor.apk",
    "sha256": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa",
    "size": 12345
  }
}
```

The checksum and size above are placeholders. Generate the real values from the **final signed APK** in your release pipeline:

```sh
sha256sum editor.apk
wc -c < editor.apk
```

On macOS, use `shasum -a 256 editor.apk`. The manifest URL must exactly match the APK's GitHub download URL. Its version must match the release version, and its size must match the GitHub asset metadata.

</Step>
<Step>

### Install and start the server

<Tabs items={["npm", "pnpm", "Yarn", "Bun"]}>

<Tab value="npm">

```sh
npm install @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-android @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="pnpm">

```sh
pnpm add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-android @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Yarn">

```sh
yarn add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-android @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Bun">

```sh
bun add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-android @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

</Tabs>

```ts title="server.ts"
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";
import { createUpserve } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { android } from "@neplex/upserve-android";

const updates = createUpserve({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [android()],
    },
  },
});

serve({ fetch: updates.fetch, port: 3000 });
```

Replace `owner/editor` with your repository, then run:

```sh
npx tsx server.ts
curl -i http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/android/update/1.0.0
```

A newer release returns the manifest with its APK URL pointing through Upserve's asset route. A current client returns `204 No Content`. `/editor/stable/android/latest.json` returns the latest manifest without a current-version comparison.

</Step>
<Step>

### Add the client update check

Have your Android client request the update URL with its current semantic version. Handle `204` as no update. For `200`, show the release notes and ask the user before downloading or installing.

Before installation, verify the downloaded file's length, SHA-256, application package name and signing certificate. Upserve checks the metadata's shape and asset size; it doesn't download and hash the APK on your behalf. Follow Android's [PackageInstaller API](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/content/pm/PackageInstaller) and the platform's permission requirements.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Manifest fields

| Field            | Type                      | Required | Meaning                                         |
| ---------------- | ------------------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `version`        | `string`                  | Yes      | Semantic version matching the release           |
| `android.url`    | `string`                  | Yes      | Exact APK download URL in the same release      |
| `android.sha256` | `string`                  | Yes      | 64 hexadecimal characters                       |
| `android.size`   | `number`                  | Yes      | Positive integer length in bytes                |
| `versionCode`    | `number`                  | No       | Positive Android version code                   |
| `notes`          | `string` or `null`        | No       | Release notes for your UI                       |
| `pub_date`       | `string`                  | No       | Publication timestamp supplied by your pipeline |
| `minimumVersion` | `string`                  | No       | Semantic version floor for your own policy      |
| `compatibility`  | `Record<string, unknown>` | No       | Your SDK, ABI or device metadata                |

## Compatibility policies

By default, Upserve compares semantic versions only. `versionCode`, `minimumVersion` and `compatibility` don't enforce an upgrade policy automatically. Your client or the `compatible` hook must interpret them.

This complete adapter definition suppresses offers for clients below a declared minimum. Add it to your application's `adapters` array instead of `android()`:

```ts title="android-adapter.ts"
import { newer, validVersion } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { android } from "@neplex/upserve-android";

export const androidAdapter = android({
  compatible(manifest, request) {
    if (!manifest.minimumVersion) return true;

    const current = request.headers.get("X-App-Version");

    return Boolean(current && validVersion(current) && !newer(manifest.minimumVersion, current));
  },
});
```

The client must send `X-App-Version` in this example. A `false` result returns `204` on either Android endpoint.

Use `android({ manifest: "updates.json" })` for a different filename. Use `transform(input)` to translate an existing format into `AndroidManifest` before validation. Treat its input as untrusted and validate fields; the hook doesn't bypass Upserve's asset checks.

## Common problems

If you receive `422`, compare the manifest version with the tag after removing `tagPrefix`, verify the SHA-256 format and confirm the APK size. The asset name must end in `.apk`. If the response is `204`, inspect the current version, channel and compatibility hook. See [troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting).


---
title: Custom applications
description: Use JSON endpoints to check versions, discover assets and build your own update client.
---

import { Tab, Tabs } from "fumadocs-ui/components/tabs";

Use `generic()` when your application doesn't need a framework-specific updater protocol. It exposes release metadata as JSON. You choose the platform asset and implement download verification and installation in your client.

## Run a generic update server

<Tabs items={["npm", "pnpm", "Yarn", "Bun"]}>

<Tab value="npm">

```sh
npm install @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="pnpm">

```sh
pnpm add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Yarn">

```sh
yarn add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Bun">

```sh
bun add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic @hono/node-server
```

</Tab>

</Tabs>

Replace `owner/editor` with your release repository.

```ts title="server.ts"
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";
import { createUpserve } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

const updates = createUpserve({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [generic()],
    },
  },
});

serve({ fetch: updates.fetch, port: 3000 });
```

```sh
npx tsx server.ts
curl -i http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/generic/update/1.0.0
```

## Read the response

A newer release returns JSON shaped like this. IDs, filenames and lengths here are illustrative; your release supplies the actual values.

```json
{
  "id": "123",
  "tag": "v1.2.0",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "prerelease": false,
  "notes": "Fixes startup on older systems.",
  "publishedAt": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "assets": [
    {
      "name": "editor-linux.tar.gz",
      "size": 12345,
      "url": "http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/assets/123/456"
    }
  ]
}
```

`notes` and `publishedAt` may be omitted. Provider-specific `metadata`, raw asset IDs and upstream asset URLs aren't included in the generic response. Asset URLs retain a parent Hono mount path if you [embed the server](/docs/embedding).

## Endpoints

All paths below start with `/editor/stable/generic`.

| Method and path          | Result                                                  |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /latest`            | Latest release, or `204` if none exists                 |
| `GET /update/:current`   | Latest release if newer than `current`, otherwise `204` |
| `GET /versions/:version` | Exact version, or `404`                                 |
| `GET /releases`          | `{ "releases": [...] }` in descending version order     |
| `GET /channels`          | `{ "channels": ["stable", "prerelease"] }` by default   |

The current version must be a semantic version such as `1.0.0`. An invalid current version returns `422` when there's a release to compare. The exact-version endpoint compares version strings, so don't include a Git tag prefix.

## A Python client

This Python 3 example checks for an update without installing anything. It uses only the standard library.

```python title="check_update.py"
import json
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

url = "http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/generic/update/1.0.0"

try:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) as response:
        if response.status == 204:
            print("You're up to date.")
        else:
            release = json.load(response)
            print(f"Version {release['version']} is available.")

            for asset in release["assets"]:
                print(f"{asset['name']}: {asset['url']}")
except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
    print(f"Update check failed: HTTP {error.code}")
except urllib.error.URLError as error:
    print(f"Update server is unavailable: {error.reason}")
```

```sh
python3 check_update.py
```

Choose an asset using a documented naming convention. The generic API doesn't infer operating systems or supply a universal checksum field. Publish a checksum/signature manifest or use a [custom adapter](/docs/custom-adapters) if your client needs one. Verify the downloaded software before executing it.

For private releases, send your application's authorization header on both metadata and asset requests. Don't put credentials in the download URL.


---
title: Applications
description: Register applications, choose update adapters and set per-application behavior.
---

Use `createUpserve()` to configure an embedded server. Use `defineConfig()` in `upserve.config.ts` for the standalone CLI. The configuration shape is the same, and `defineConfig()` gives you autocomplete and type checking.

```ts title="upserve.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { tauri } from "@neplex/upserve-tauri";
import { android } from "@neplex/upserve-android";

export default defineConfig({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [tauri(), android()],
    },
  },
});
```

This application exposes Tauri and Android endpoints below `/editor/stable` and `/editor/prerelease`. Register another entry in `apps` to serve a second application with its own provider and policies.

For this configuration, install `@neplex/upserve`, `@neplex/upserve-github`, `@neplex/upserve-tauri` and `@neplex/upserve-android`, plus `@neplex/upserve-cli` if you're using the CLI. The [quick start](/docs/quick-start) shows how to serve an embedded configuration.

## Common application options

| Option      | Type                                                | Required              | Default                    | Use it to                                        |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `provider`  | `Provider`                                          | Yes                   | None                       | Choose where releases come from                  |
| `adapters`  | `Adapter[]`                                         | Yes                   | None                       | Expose the update protocols you need             |
| `channels`  | `Record<string, (release: Release) => boolean>`     | No                    | `stable` and `prerelease`  | Select releases for each channel                 |
| `authorize` | `(request: Request) => boolean \| Promise<boolean>` | For private providers | No access check            | Decide who can read metadata and download assets |
| `cache`     | `CachePolicy`                                       | No                    | See [caching](/docs/cache) | Change metadata lifetimes for this application   |
| `delivery`  | `"redirect" \| "stream"`                            | No                    | Redirect when supported    | Send public downloads through your server        |

App and channel names become URL segments. Start them with a letter or number, then use letters, numbers, `.`, `_` or `-`, up to 128 characters. Adapter names must be unique within an application.

## Keep the first configuration small

For a public repository, start with `provider` and `adapters`. You don't need custom cache keys, a persistent store or authorization to try Upserve.

Add [authentication](/docs/security) for private releases, [custom channels](/docs/channels) when you publish beta builds, or [SQLite](/docs/cache#persist-metadata-with-sqlite) when you want cached metadata to survive a restart.

## Advanced server options

The top-level `cache` chooses a store for the server; `apps.editor.cache` controls lifetimes. These are different options. `namespace`, `concurrency`, `background` and `now` are also top-level options. See the [configuration reference](/docs/configuration-reference) for their defaults and examples.

Configuration files and plugins execute as trusted code. Only load configuration you control.


---
title: Release channels
description: Select stable, prerelease and custom release streams using semantic versions.
---

Channels decide which releases an endpoint can see. They don't create releases or change the files you've published.

With the default configuration:

| Channel      | Included releases                                |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `stable`     | Releases whose provider sets `prerelease: false` |
| `prerelease` | Releases whose provider sets `prerelease: true`  |

For GitHub, this flag comes from the release's **Set as a pre-release** setting. It is separate from whether the tag contains a suffix such as `-beta.1`. Keep the tag and GitHub setting consistent so a beta doesn't enter your stable channel.

## Define your own channels

The `channels` object replaces both defaults. Include `stable` yourself if you still want it.

```ts title="upserve.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

export default defineConfig({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [generic()],
      channels: {
        stable: (release) => !release.prerelease,
        beta: (release) => release.prerelease && release.version.includes("-beta."),
      },
    },
  },
});
```

Request `/editor/beta/generic/latest` to check that selection. Channel predicates can inspect the normalized release, including provider-specific `metadata`, but should stay synchronous and avoid network work.

## Which release wins?

Upserve removes drafts and yanked releases, sorts the remaining releases by semantic version, then applies your channel predicate. `1.10.0` sorts above `1.9.0`, and `1.0.0-beta.10` sorts above `1.0.0-beta.2`. Publication order doesn't decide the winner. Build metadata such as `+build.5` doesn't increase version precedence.

The selected release must contain the manifest and artifacts for the adapter you're using. An invalid newest release produces an error; it doesn't automatically fall back to an older one.

## Tags aren't versions

The GitHub provider removes `v` by default: `v1.2.0` becomes `1.2.0`. Use `tagPrefix: "editor-v"` for `editor-v1.2.0`, or `tagPrefix: ""` for bare `1.2.0` tags. Tags that don't match the prefix and a valid semantic version are ignored.

Changing a channel predicate while reusing a cache is safe for selection because predicates run after metadata is loaded. Changing repository credentials needs a new [cache scope](/docs/security#cache-isolation), not just a different channel name.


---
title: GitHub Releases
description: Connect a public or private repository and understand tag matching and upstream requests.
---

Use the GitHub provider to read published releases and their assets. Start with a public repository and add authentication only if you need it.

Install `@neplex/upserve-github` alongside `@neplex/upserve` and your adapter packages. The [quick start](/docs/quick-start) includes a complete running server.

```ts title="provider.ts"
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";

export const provider = github({
  repository: "owner/editor",
  tagPrefix: "v",
});
```

`repository` is an `owner/repository` pair, not a URL. Replace `owner/editor`. With the default prefix `v`, a tag `v1.2.0` produces version `1.2.0`. Use `tagPrefix: "editor-v"` for `editor-v1.2.0`, or an empty string for bare versions.

## Prepare your releases

Publish a release with a valid semantic version tag. Upload your adapter's original manifest and every artifact it references to that release. GitHub's source archives aren't a replacement for your application's updater artifacts.

Upserve scans the release list instead of relying on GitHub's latest-release endpoint. It can therefore select stable and prerelease channels independently and order by semantic version. Drafts aren't offered. See [channels](/docs/channels) for prerelease selection.

## Authenticate with GitHub

Pass a token from your environment as `token`. For private repositories, use a read-only credential with access to repository contents. See GitHub's [release API permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/releases/releases#list-releases) for the token type you're using.

A token enables private mode by default, which requires downstream authorization. Read [private releases](/docs/security) before adding one. Set `private: false` only when you're deliberately authenticating API requests for a **public** repository.

The official provider uses `api.github.com` and GitHub's release asset hosts. It doesn't accept a custom API origin or support GitHub Enterprise. Implement a [custom provider](/docs/custom-providers) for another host.

## Requests and rate limits

Upserve reuses cached GitHub pages rather than requesting them for every client check. When a page needs refreshing, its saved ETag and Last-Modified values become conditional request headers. A `304 Not Modified` reuses the previous page body.

The provider fetches 100 releases per page, up to 20 pages by default. If all configured pages are full, it reports a pagination-limit error instead of silently omitting history. Increase `maxPages` if needed; the maximum is 100. This bounds release lookup and old blockmap searches.

Network and server errors get two retries by default, using exponential backoff with jitter. Rate-limit responses establish a cooldown instead of repeated retries. GitHub's `Retry-After` and reset time influence when requests resume. A secondary-limit message without those headers pauses requests for one minute. Other `403` responses are treated as access failures. See [caching and rate limits](/docs/cache) for what your clients receive.

## Options you may need

| Option          | Type      | Required | Default                                  | Change it when                                                              |
| --------------- | --------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `repository`    | `string`  | Yes      | None                                     | Selecting the GitHub repository                                             |
| `tagPrefix`     | `string`  | No       | `"v"`                                    | Your tags use a different prefix                                            |
| `token`         | `string`  | No       | None                                     | Reading a private repository or authenticating public API requests          |
| `private`       | `boolean` | No       | `Boolean(token)`                         | Explicitly distinguishing public authenticated access from private releases |
| `webhookSecret` | `string`  | No       | None                                     | Enabling [release webhooks](/docs/webhooks)                                 |
| `timeout`       | `number`  | No       | `30_000` ms                              | Downloads need more than 30 seconds                                         |
| `maxPages`      | `number`  | No       | `20`                                     | Release history exceeds the page limit                                      |
| `retries`       | `number`  | No       | `2`                                      | Tuning network/5xx retries, from `0` to `5`                                 |
| `cacheScope`    | `string`  | No       | Random for tokens; `anonymous` otherwise | Reusing persistent data across restarts with a stable credential generation |

For test injection options `fetch`, `sleep` and `random`, see the [API reference](/docs/api#githuboptions).


---
title: Authentication and security
description: Protect private release metadata and downloads without exposing GitHub credentials.
---

import { Callout } from "fumadocs-ui/components/callout";

<Callout type="warn">

Giving Upserve a GitHub token lets it access your repository. It doesn't give your application users permission to download private releases. You configure that access separately.

</Callout>

## Protect a private application

A GitHub token implies `private: true` unless you override it. Private providers require an `authorize(request)` callback; Upserve refuses to create the application without one. Requests denied by that callback return `401` before any release lookup or download.

This standalone example uses Hono's constant-time comparison utility for a server-managed bearer credential. Install `hono` along with the CLI, core, GitHub and generic packages. Supply both environment values before starting the service.

```ts title="upserve.config.ts"
import { timingSafeEqual } from "hono/utils/buffer";
import { defineConfig } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

const githubToken = process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN;
const clientToken = process.env.UPDATE_CLIENT_TOKEN;

if (!githubToken || !clientToken) {
  throw new Error("GITHUB_TOKEN and UPDATE_CLIENT_TOKEN are required");
}

export default defineConfig({
  namespace: "editor-private-v1",
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({
        repository: "owner/editor",
        token: githubToken,
        cacheScope: "read-credential-generation-1",
      }),
      adapters: [generic()],
      authorize: (request) =>
        timingSafeEqual(request.headers.get("Authorization") ?? "", `Bearer ${clientToken}`),
    },
  },
});
```

Use your existing authentication or entitlement verification for production applications. A shared token embedded in a distributed app can be extracted; it isn't an individual user identity. The callback can be asynchronous so you can verify your own credentials without adding an authentication system to Upserve.

Send the downstream credential on **both** metadata and asset requests:

```sh
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $UPDATE_CLIENT_TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/generic/latest
```

Do not send your GitHub token to application clients. Private assets always stream through Upserve; responses use `Cache-Control: private, no-store` when application authorization is configured.

## Authenticated public repositories

If your repository is public and you only need authenticated API access, explicitly set `private: false` in `github()`. This permits public metadata and redirects. Never use that setting to bypass private-repository access checks.

## Cache isolation

`namespace` separates deployments in a shared cache. The provider's `scope` separates repository/configuration and credential generations. GitHub includes its repository and tag prefix, and uses a random scope for authenticated providers unless you set `cacheScope`.

For persistent reuse, set a nonsecret `cacheScope` that identifies a credential generation. Change it when you rotate credentials or change their permissions. Change the deployment namespace when you change the broader security boundary. Never use a token as either value.

Authentication failures discovered during refresh clear the affected cache entry. Fresh cached data isn't a live check of GitHub permissions, and background refresh can return stale data before a revocation is detected. Keep downstream authorization active and use finite cache lifetimes. See [caching](/docs/cache#authentication-failures-are-different).

## Downloads and network boundaries

Only registered release assets can be downloaded. The official GitHub provider validates repository download URLs and follows API redirects only to its allowed GitHub asset hosts. Credentials go to `api.github.com`, not redirect destinations or client-visible URLs.

Custom providers must implement their own URL and redirect policy. Support for a deliberate private-network source belongs in that provider's explicit configuration. It mustn't become an arbitrary URL proxy. See [custom providers](/docs/custom-providers).

## Deploy safely

- Use HTTPS and configure your reverse proxy to accept only your canonical host. Generated asset URLs use the request origin.
- Forward authorization headers and disable CDN caching for protected routes.
- Rate limit public traffic at the edge, especially downloads. Metadata refresh coordination isn't a general client rate limiter.
- Keep signing private keys in your release pipeline. Upserve doesn't need them.
- Load only trusted plugins and TypeScript configurations. They run as application code and aren't sandboxed.

For vulnerability reports, follow the repository's [security policy](https://github.com/neplextech/upserve/blob/main/SECURITY.md). Don't include credentials or private download links in public reports.


---
title: Caching and rate limits
description: Understand what clients receive when metadata expires, GitHub fails or a release changes.
---

Suppose several hundred installed copies of Editor check for updates at startup. If each one asks GitHub directly, they all consume API requests for the same release information. With Upserve, those clients share cached metadata.

The first check loads the release list. Checks during the fresh period reuse it. If many clients arrive together when it expires, Upserve performs one refresh for that data and shares the result. This is called **request coalescing**: a burst of checks doesn't become a burst of identical GitHub requests.

## What gets cached

Upserve caches normalized release lists, provider resources such as GitHub API pages, and validated adapter manifests. It doesn't store installers, APKs or blockmaps. Those files redirect to the upstream or stream through your server.

The default store holds up to 1,000 metadata entries in memory. Restarting the process clears it. Use [SQLite](#persist-metadata-with-sqlite) if you need cached metadata after a restart.

## Default timing

All cache options are in **milliseconds** and apply per application.

| Option         | Default                  | Meaning                                                             |
| -------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ttl`          | `60_000` (one minute)    | How long successful metadata stays fresh                            |
| `negativeTtl`  | `15_000` (15 seconds)    | How long a confirmed empty release list stays fresh                 |
| `staleIfError` | `300_000` (five minutes) | How long previously validated data can be used after freshness ends |

For a release list loaded at 12:00:00 with these defaults:

| Time                                   | What a check does                                                        |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Before 12:01:00                        | Uses the fresh cached list                                               |
| At or after 12:01:00                   | Tries to refresh before answering, unless you enabled background refresh |
| During an outage, before 12:06:00      | Can answer with the old list if refresh fails                            |
| During an outage, at or after 12:06:00 | Returns an error because the old list has expired completely             |

This is **stale-if-error**: old but validated metadata can bridge a short outage. It isn't an unlimited fallback. Each resource has its own timestamps, so manifest and list expiry can differ.

## When GitHub is unavailable

If GitHub fails and Upserve has usable cached metadata, the client can still get an update response until the stale window ends. A malformed refresh doesn't replace the previous validated data.

If GitHub is unavailable and nothing is cached yet, the update endpoint returns an error, usually `503 Service Unavailable`. A malformed response can return `422`. Upserve records a refresh cooldown so the next client doesn't immediately repeat the failed request. The default cooldown for failures without a provider deadline is 15 seconds.

A successful **empty** release list means no releases exist. It replaces the previous list and uses the shorter `negativeTtl`. This is **negative caching**: Upserve remembers that nothing was found without treating an outage as an empty repository.

## When GitHub rate limits requests

The GitHub provider reads `Retry-After` and rate-limit reset headers and pauses further upstream work until the deadline. It also recognizes secondary throttling responses. During that pause, clients can use metadata still inside its stale window. Otherwise they receive `503` with an error code and, when available, a `Retry-After` header.

Don't invalidate the cache in a client retry loop. That won't override a provider cooldown and removes data that might have kept your update checks working. Let clients retry later and use [webhooks](/docs/webhooks) for release changes.

## Authentication failures are different

When a refresh reports an upstream authentication error, Upserve clears the affected cached entry instead of serving it as an outage fallback. The request reports an error, and later checks respect the cooldown.

This isn't an immediate credential-revocation check on every client request. Fresh data can be served until refresh discovers the problem. With background refresh enabled, the request that starts the refresh can receive stale data before that failure is known. Enforce user access in `authorize()` on every request and rotate cache scopes when permissions change.

## Change the lifetimes

For an app that rarely publishes and can tolerate a longer update delay:

```ts title="upserve.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

export default defineConfig({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [generic()],
      cache: {
        ttl: 5 * 60 * 1000,
        negativeTtl: 15 * 1000,
        staleIfError: 10 * 60 * 1000,
      },
    },
  },
});
```

This keeps metadata fresh for five minutes and allows ten additional minutes during errors. Shorten `ttl` when update latency matters; keep a finite stale window that fits your release withdrawal policy. A longer TTL also means a deleted or withdrawn release can remain visible longer.

## Make new releases available

There are no automatic polling timers. By default, the first request after expiry refreshes metadata. Configure an [authenticated GitHub webhook](/docs/webhooks) to refresh after a release event.

Embedded applications can call `await updates.refresh("editor")`. This revalidates the release list and provider page resources even when they're fresh, while respecting cooldowns. It doesn't invalidate every adapter manifest. If you replace a manifest on an existing release, its own TTL still matters.

`await updates.invalidate("editor")` removes the resolved release-list entry. The next check reloads it, but invalidation doesn't remove every provider resource or manifest. Use these methods only from trusted server code; Upserve has no public force-refresh query parameter or admin endpoint.

A successful refresh removes deleted and yanked releases from selection. An invalid newest manifest causes an error rather than falling back to an older release. Prefer immutable release artifacts and publish a new version to correct a bad update.

## Refresh in the background

If your host can keep work alive after responding, supply `background(task)`. Upserve can then return usable stale data immediately and refresh it in the background. This is **stale-while-revalidate**.

Without this option, checks wait for the refresh and need no long-lived timer or background runtime support. Don't pass a fire-and-forget callback on a host that can terminate work after the response. See [runtime guidance](/docs/embedding#other-fetch-based-runtimes).

## Persist metadata with SQLite

Install `@neplex/upserve-sqlite` alongside your server packages. It uses Node's built-in SQLite module and isn't a Workers cache.

```ts title="persistent-config.ts"
import { mkdir } from "node:fs/promises";
import { defineConfig } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";
import { sqliteCache } from "@neplex/upserve-sqlite";

await mkdir("./data", { recursive: true });

export const cache = sqliteCache("./data/metadata.sqlite");

export default defineConfig({
  namespace: "editor-production-v1",
  cache,
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [generic()],
    },
  },
});
```

Close the store with `cache.close()` after requests drain. The CLI can manage this for you when you set `UPSERVE_CACHE_DIR`; see [deployment](/docs/deployment).

SQLite uses WAL mode and persists metadata and timestamps. It doesn't automatically prune old rows or cache binaries. Monitor disk use, especially if you change namespaces or publish many releases.

## Advanced coordination and isolation

Each Upserve instance coordinates its own refreshes. A shared store doesn't add distributed locks, a global GitHub rate-limit budget or a shared concurrency limit. Multiple processes can refresh the same data simultaneously. Use one instance per credential scope if you need that coordination guarantee.

The default concurrency is four per coordination pool, with separate pools for resolved data and provider resources. It isn't a four-request limit for all downloads. See [configuration options](/docs/configuration-reference).

Cache keys separate deployments, applications, providers and provider scopes. Channels filter the app's shared release list. GitHub page validators are saved with the page: a later conditional request can use ETag or Last-Modified and reuse a `304` response. See [private cache isolation](/docs/security#cache-isolation) before sharing persistent storage.

Client metadata responses also have ETags. Public metadata requires revalidation; protected responses use `private, no-store`. HTTP caching at your CDN is a separate policy from Upserve's server-side metadata cache.


---
title: Asset delivery
description: Choose redirects or streaming and configure large or differential downloads.
---

Upserve separates metadata caching from binary delivery. A cached update response doesn't mean the installer is stored on your server.

## Redirect public downloads

Public GitHub assets redirect by default. Upserve validates the known asset URL and returns `302` to the GitHub release download path. The client follows GitHub's own download redirects. This keeps installer traffic off your server.

Only registered assets can be requested. Clients can't provide an arbitrary URL for Upserve to proxy.

## Stream through Upserve

Set `delivery: "stream"` on an application when downloads should pass through your server. Private providers always stream, regardless of that setting.

```ts title="upserve.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

export default defineConfig({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({
        repository: "owner/editor",
        timeout: 5 * 60 * 1000,
      }),
      adapters: [generic()],
      delivery: "stream",
    },
  },
});
```

This gives each upstream request up to five minutes. The GitHub default is 30 seconds, including streamed response consumption in standard Fetch implementations. Increase it for large installers and slow links, and check your proxy's timeout too.

Streaming uses Web Streams and doesn't load the whole installer into memory. The upstream receives the client's cancellation signal. Stream backpressure allows the downstream's read speed to control consumption.

## Resume and differential downloads

GitHub asset streaming supports `GET` and `HEAD`. It forwards `Range`, `If-Range`, `If-None-Match` and `If-Modified-Since`, and preserves upstream `200`, `206`, `304` and `416` statuses. It retains download headers including length, media type, disposition, content range, ETag and Last-Modified.

Use an actual asset URL returned by a manifest or generic response:

```sh
curl -I "$ASSET_URL"
curl -D - -H 'Range: bytes=0-1023' "$ASSET_URL" -o first-kib.bin
```

For a valid range, expect `206 Partial Content` and a matching `Content-Range`. Add your downstream authorization header for private releases.

Electron-updater uses these requests with blockmaps to reduce download size. Configure single-range requests for GitHub and keep old blockmaps available; see [Electron](/docs/electron#differential-downloads). Upserve doesn't generate differential data or guarantee multipart ranges.

## Reverse proxies and CDNs

Forward `Range`, conditional and authorization headers. Preserve partial-response statuses and headers, and disable response buffering for large streamed downloads.

Public streamed assets use a one-hour HTTP cache lifetime. Protected streams use `private, no-store`. Don't let a CDN override private cache controls. Treat public artifact URLs as immutable, especially when enabling an external CDN.

A CDN or binary mirror can be added independently, but Upserve has no built-in persistent binary storage. Never rewrite checksums or signature contents just to change a download location.


---
title: Release webhooks
description: Refresh a GitHub application after authenticated release events.
---

A webhook makes newly published releases available without waiting for the next expired-cache request. GitHub sends a signed event, and Upserve verifies it before refreshing the application's release list.

## Configure the secret

Generate a long random secret and store it in both your server environment and GitHub's webhook configuration. Don't commit it.

```ts title="upserve.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

const webhookSecret = process.env.GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET;

if (!webhookSecret) throw new Error("GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET is required");

export default defineConfig({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor", webhookSecret }),
      adapters: [generic()],
    },
  },
});
```

This example assumes a public repository. Add repository credentials and downstream authorization separately if needed.

## Add the GitHub webhook

In your repository's **Settings → Webhooks**, create a webhook with:

| Setting      | Value                                         |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| Payload URL  | `https://updates.example.com/webhooks/editor` |
| Content type | `application/json`                            |
| Secret       | The value of `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`          |
| Events       | Release events                                |

Replace the host and application ID. If Upserve is mounted at `/updates`, use `/updates/webhooks/editor` instead.

Upserve verifies the HMAC-SHA256 signature, the `release` event type and `repository.full_name`. It accepts release events regardless of their action and refreshes from GitHub rather than trusting the event's release data.

## Test a delivery

Use GitHub's webhook delivery history to inspect a real event or redeliver a signed release event. A successful refresh responds:

```json
{ "refreshed": true }
```

A missing or incorrect signature, wrong repository or unsupported event type returns `401`. GitHub's initial `ping` event isn't a release event, so it also returns `401`. That doesn't mean release signature verification is broken.

Bodies are limited to 256 KiB. Valid deliveries are limited to one refresh per application every ten seconds in each process; faster deliveries return `429`. If the refresh fails, the response uses the normal [error format](/docs/errors).

## What a webhook refreshes

The event forces release-list and provider-page revalidation while respecting upstream cooldowns. It doesn't purge every cached adapter manifest. Publish immutable artifacts in new releases instead of replacing a manifest in place.

Webhook access uses its signature, not your application's `authorize()` callback. Don't add an open refresh route for clients. For trusted scheduled work in an embedded server, use `updates.refresh("editor")` directly.


---
title: Standalone CLI and Docker
description: Run Upserve as a service with typed configuration, health checks and persistent metadata.
---

import { Tab, Tabs } from "fumadocs-ui/components/tabs";

Use the CLI if you want a standalone service. You don't need to write an HTTP listener. For an existing server, see [embedding in Hono, Node.js and Bun](/docs/embedding).

## Install the CLI

Use Node.js 24 for the service and SQLite cache. Install the packages your configuration imports too:

<Tabs items={["npm", "pnpm", "Yarn", "Bun"]}>

<Tab value="npm">

```sh
npm install @neplex/upserve-cli @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="pnpm">

```sh
pnpm add @neplex/upserve-cli @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Yarn">

```sh
yarn add @neplex/upserve-cli @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Bun">

```sh
bun add @neplex/upserve-cli @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

</Tab>

</Tabs>

```sh
npx upserve init
```

This creates `upserve.config.ts` and refuses to overwrite an existing file. The executable is `upserve`; you can also run `pnpm exec upserve`, `yarn upserve` or `bunx upserve` after installation.

## Configuration file

Edit the generated file. Use `editor` consistently as the application ID and replace `owner/editor` with your repository.

```ts title="upserve.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

export default defineConfig({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [generic()],
    },
  },
});
```

```sh
npx upserve start
```

The service prints structured JSON, including a line like:

```json
{ "time": "2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z", "event": "listening", "port": 3000 }
```

Check it from another terminal:

```sh
curl http://localhost:3000/health/ready
curl -i http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/generic/latest
```

Readiness returns `{"status":"ready"}`. The second request tests your release source; health endpoints don't contact GitHub.

## Environment variables

| Variable            | Default             | Purpose                                                 |
| ------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `UPSERVE_CONFIG`    | `upserve.config.ts` | Path to your trusted TypeScript configuration           |
| `HOST`              | `0.0.0.0`           | Listener address; use `127.0.0.1` for local-only access |
| `PORT`              | `3000`              | Listener port, integer from 1 to 65535                  |
| `UPSERVE_CACHE_DIR` | Unset               | Directory for `metadata.sqlite`; created if needed      |

Set `UPSERVE_CACHE_DIR=./data` to enable persistent metadata unless your configuration already supplies a cache. The CLI opens and closes that SQLite store for you. It doesn't delete old entries automatically.

Secrets such as `GITHUB_TOKEN` are read by **your configuration**, not automatically applied by the CLI. Upserve doesn't load `.env` files for you. Pass values through your shell, process manager or container environment. See [authentication](/docs/security) before adding a GitHub token.

On `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`, the service marks readiness as draining, stops accepting connections and allows up to ten seconds for requests to finish. Downloads that exceed the drain deadline can be interrupted. Liveness at `/health/live` returns `{"status":"ok"}`.

## Docker Compose

During initial development, build the image from the repository. No published image is assumed:

```sh
docker build -t upserve .
```

The repository's Compose file builds this image, mounts `examples/upserve.config.ts` and stores metadata in a named volume. Edit that configuration first, then run:

```sh
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose logs -f upserve
curl http://localhost:3000/health/ready
```

The image runs Node.js as UID/GID `10001`, listens on port `3000`, reads `/config/upserve.config.ts` and stores SQLite data under `/data`. Bind-mounted data directories must be writable by that user. Custom configuration imports must be installed in the image; mounting a config file doesn't install extra dependencies.

## Coolify

Select a Dockerfile deployment from this repository, expose port `3000`, mount persistent storage at `/data`, and mount your configuration at `/config/upserve.config.ts`. Configure environment secrets in Coolify. Use `/health/ready` for the health check and your platform's HTTPS proxy for the public domain.

You don't need PostgreSQL or Redis. One process is the simplest deployment when you want all update checks to share refresh coordination.

## Reverse proxy configuration

Terminate HTTPS at your proxy and accept only the intended host. Upserve builds asset URLs from the incoming origin, so verify generated URLs use the public HTTPS host in your environment. Forward authorization, range and conditional headers, preserve `206` responses, and disable buffering for streamed downloads. Never cache private routes at the CDN.

Upserve doesn't start a polling timer. Checks refresh expired metadata as needed; [GitHub webhooks](/docs/webhooks) can refresh release lists after publication. Don't expose the programmatic refresh methods as unauthenticated HTTP routes.


---
title: Hono, Node.js and Bun
description: Mount Upserve in an existing Hono app or run its Fetch handler in your runtime.
---

import { Tab, Tabs } from "fumadocs-ui/components/tabs";

`createUpserve()` returns a Hono application. You can use its Fetch handler directly or mount it in another Hono app. The library doesn't start a server, open a database or create timers on its own.

## Hono on Node.js

<Tabs items={["npm", "pnpm", "Yarn", "Bun"]}>

<Tab value="npm">

```sh
npm install hono @hono/node-server @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="pnpm">

```sh
pnpm add hono @hono/node-server @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Yarn">

```sh
yarn add hono @hono/node-server @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

</Tab>

<Tab value="Bun">

```sh
bun add hono @hono/node-server @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

</Tab>

</Tabs>

```ts title="server.ts"
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { serve } from "@hono/node-server";
import { createUpserve } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

const updates = createUpserve({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [generic()],
    },
  },
});

const app = new Hono();

app.get("/", (context) => context.text("Editor service"));
app.route("/updates", updates);

serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 });
```

```sh
npx tsx server.ts
curl http://localhost:3000/updates/editor/stable/generic/channels
```

Returned asset URLs retain `/updates`. For a dedicated Node.js listener, pass `updates.fetch` to `serve()` directly, as in the [quick start](/docs/quick-start). See [Hono's Node adapter guide](https://hono.dev/docs/getting-started/nodejs) for server options.

## Bun

Install the core, GitHub and generic packages; Bun supplies the HTTP server, so you don't need `@hono/node-server`.

```sh
bun add @neplex/upserve @neplex/upserve-github @neplex/upserve-generic
```

```ts title="server.bun.ts"
import { createUpserve } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { github } from "@neplex/upserve-github";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";

const updates = createUpserve({
  apps: {
    editor: {
      provider: github({ repository: "owner/editor" }),
      adapters: [generic()],
    },
  },
});

Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch: updates.fetch });
```

```sh
bun run server.bun.ts
curl http://localhost:3000/editor/stable/generic/channels
```

## Other Fetch-based runtimes

The core uses Fetch, Web Crypto, AbortSignal and Web Streams rather than Node APIs. A Fetch host can call `updates.fetch(request)`. The repository includes a Worker integration example, but it hasn't been deployed and validated on Cloudflare. Treat it as a starting point to test in your own environment, not a claim of verified production compatibility.

Without `background`, expired-cache requests await refresh and don't depend on work continuing after the response. Hosts with a `waitUntil()` facility can pass a callback as `background: (task) => context.waitUntil(task)` when creating Upserve in the appropriate request scope. Don't capture an expired request context in a long-lived instance. Constructing a new instance per request also loses process-local coalescing between requests; choose your lifecycle deliberately.

SQLite and the standalone CLI are Node-specific. Use memory or a [custom cache store](/docs/custom-cache-stores) in other runtimes.

## What is validated

The repository's runtime smoke script exercises built package entry points on Node.js and Bun. Protocol tests use the Hono Fetch handler directly. This doesn't prove installation behavior on every desktop OS, a Workers deployment or every serverless host.

When embedding, you own listener shutdown, logs and health routes. The CLI's `/health/*` endpoints aren't added to the core application. See [standalone deployment](/docs/deployment) if you want those lifecycle features included.


---
title: Extend Upserve
description: Choose the extension point for a new release source, update protocol or metadata store.
---

You can add a release source, update protocol or cache store without changing Upserve. Official integrations use the same public contracts available to your code.

| You want to change                          | Implement    | Start here                                       |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Where release metadata and assets come from | `Provider`   | [Custom providers](/docs/custom-providers)       |
| What routes and responses your updater uses | `Adapter`    | [Custom adapters](/docs/custom-adapters)         |
| Where cached metadata is saved              | `CacheStore` | [Custom cache stores](/docs/custom-cache-stores) |

Start with the smallest contract that fits your task. For example, a new JSON response format usually needs an adapter, not a new provider. Your adapter can reuse GitHub and the existing cache.

The `defineProvider()`, `defineAdapter()` and `defineCache()` helpers check the contract while preserving your object's inferred properties. They don't wrap or sandbox your code. Plugins run with the application's permissions, so only install integrations you trust.

Each guide below includes a complete implementation and a deterministic test. The [API reference](/docs/api#extension-contracts) documents the full method signatures and shared services.


---
title: Custom providers
description: Implement and test a release source using the public Provider contract.
---

Write a provider when your releases live somewhere other than GitHub, or when you want to supply a catalog you already maintain. A provider returns normalized releases and opens their known assets. It doesn't define HTTP update routes.

Upserve handles channel selection, release validation, metadata lifetimes and request coalescing. Your provider handles access to the source, source-specific validation, credentials and safe asset delivery.

## 1. Return a small catalog

Install `@neplex/upserve` and `@neplex/upserve-generic`. This complete provider serves a fixed metadata-only release. It deliberately publishes no assets, so it needs no network access and is easy to test.

```ts title="catalog-provider.ts"
import { defineProvider, UpserveError } from "@neplex/upserve";
import type { Release } from "@neplex/upserve";

export function catalogProvider() {
  const releases: Release[] = [
    {
      id: "release-12",
      tag: "v1.2.0",
      version: "1.2.0",
      prerelease: false,
      notes: "Fixes startup on older systems.",
      assets: [],
    },
  ];

  return defineProvider({
    name: "catalog",
    scope: "editor-catalog-v1",

    async releases() {
      return structuredClone(releases);
    },

    async open() {
      throw new UpserveError("missing", "This catalog has no downloadable assets");
    },
  });
}
```

`id` is a stable source identifier, `tag` is the original reference, and `version` is a semantic version used for comparison. Don't put a tag such as `editor-v1.2.0` into `version`.

## 2. Register and test it

Install `vitest` as a development dependency. Save this next to `catalog-provider.ts` and run `npx vitest run catalog-provider.test.ts`:

```ts title="catalog-provider.test.ts"
import { expect, it } from "vitest";
import { createUpserve } from "@neplex/upserve";
import { generic } from "@neplex/upserve-generic";
import { catalogProvider } from "./catalog-provider.js";

it("serves the catalog through the generic adapter", async () => {
  const updates = createUpserve({
    apps: {
      editor: { provider: catalogProvider(), adapters: [generic()] },
    },
  });

  const response = await updates.request("/editor/stable/generic/latest");
  const release = await response.json();

  expect(response.status).toBe(200);
  expect(release.version).toBe("1.2.0");
  expect(release.assets).toEqual([]);
});
```

The same configuration can be passed to the CLI or a [runtime listener](/docs/embedding). Replace `generic()` with any adapter once your source publishes that adapter's required manifests and artifacts.

## 3. Load from a real source

Replace the fixed array with your source request. Accept `context` in `releases(context)` and use `context.cached("catalog-page", loader)` for reusable source resources. The loader receives its previous cached value, which can include an ETag or Last-Modified validator.

Validate the source response **inside the loader before returning it**. On a conditional `304`, return the previous validated value. For JSON, use `readText(response, maxBytes)` to bound the body before parsing. A source that pages results must enforce its own page limit.

Return `[]` only when the source confirms there are no releases. Throw `UpserveError("network", "Source unavailable")` for temporary failures, `"invalid"` for malformed metadata, `"auth"` for rejected credentials or `"rate_limit"` with an absolute `retryAt` timestamp for throttling. Never include tokens or raw source error bodies in messages.

## 4. Add asset delivery

For each real asset, return its stable `id`, unique `name`, byte `size` and safe `url`. Implement `open(asset, request, context)` to fetch only that known asset.
